hook: Request/response is a letter; realtime is a phone call. **WebSockets give your FastAPI apps a live wire — streaming LLM tokens, chat, dashboards — and webhooks give the outside world a way to call YOU.**

scenes.title: WebSockets: one TCP connection, both directions, forever
scenes.sub: HTTP asks and answers; WebSocket converses
scenes.narration: HTTP's limitation for live apps is structural: the client must ASK for everything — polling wastes bandwidth and freshness; long-polling hacks the gap. WebSockets upgrade the same HTTP connection — literally: the client sends an Upgrade request, the server answers 101 Switching Protocols, and from that moment the connection is a full-duplex pipe — either side pushes anytime, for as long as it lives. Key mechanics: MESSAGES not requests — the wire is frames, not HTTP envelopes; order is guaranteed but delivery is NOT — a dropped connection means lost messages unless your protocol acknowledges (you build that layer); and state is per-CONNECTION — the server keeps an in-memory object per client — which is why WebSocket servers scale by connection count, not request count. In FastAPI, an endpoint becomes a websocket endpoint with one decorator, and you send/receive with two calls — the entire API surface. The mental model from earlier reels: HTTP is AG-19's job queue (discrete, retriable tasks); WebSocket is the agent's live phone line (GA-28's realtime voice).

scenes.title: The WebSocket handshake and echo
scenes.body:
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def ws(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()          # completes the 101 upgrade
    try:
        while True:
            msg = await websocket.receive_text()
            await websocket.send_text(f"echo: {msg}")
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        pass                          # client went away — normal

# The handshake, decoded:
#   client → GET /ws  Upgrade: websocket   (asks to switch)
#   server → 101 Switching Protocols       (pipe is open)
# after that: NO more HTTP. frames both ways.
#
# Python client:
#   async with websockets.connect("ws://host/ws") as ws:
#       await ws.send("hello")
#       reply = await ws.recv()
annot: accept() completes the upgrade — before it, the connection is still pretending to be HTTP
receive_text blocks forever — the while-True loop IS the connection's lifetime
WebSocketDisconnect is the normal exit path — close happens, plan for it

scenes.title: Connection managers, rooms, and the killer app: token streaming
scenes.sub: The two patterns every realtime backend is made of
scenes.narration: Pattern one: the CONNECTION MANAGER — because everything interesting involves MORE than two parties. A manager tracks live sockets — usually keyed by user or session ID in a dict — and provides broadcast: send to one, send to a room, send to all. Rooms are just key → set-of-sockets maps; chat channels, document collab, live dashboards are all the same shape underneath. Pattern two — and the reason this reel exists in a GenAI course: TOKEN STREAMING. LLM answers arrive token-by-token (GA-07); piping them straight to a WebSocket gives users text that appears as it's THOUGHT — the single biggest perceived-latency win in GenAI UI. The wiring: POST endpoint starts the job → the LLM's async stream is forwarded to the client's socket → done sentinel closes the stream (not the socket). Async is load-bearing here: while one client's LLM call streams over seconds, the same process must serve every other client — never block the event loop on a slow generation; each connection is an independent async task, and asyncio.gather runs them all on one thread.

scenes.title: Connection manager + LLM token streaming
annot: rooms: dict[str, set] — broadcast is a loop over a set; that's the whole pattern
Prune dead sockets on send-failure — silent disconnects otherwise leak memory
'[DONE]' sentinel vs closing the socket — protocol on top of the wire: you define it

scenes.title: Webhooks: the outside world's way of calling your app
scenes.sub: HTTP inverted — events arrive as POSTs; trust nothing
scenes.narration: WebSockets push YOUR server → YOUR client; WEBHOOKS push SOMEONE ELSE's server → yours: Stripe posts charge.succeeded, GitHub posts push events, the LLM provider posts a completed job — any time an external system must tell you something happened. Architecturally it's an endpoint plus a contract: the provider documents the payload shape and a SIGNING SECRET; your endpoint MUST verify every delivery — recompute the HMAC signature over the raw body with the secret, compare in constant time, reject mismatches — an unverified webhook endpoint is an open door where anyone POSTs 'payment received' (AG-23's trust-nothing discipline, inbound edition). Reliability mechanics, the same trio as AG-19: IDEMPOTENCY — providers REDELIVER on timeout, so dedupe by event ID; FAST ACK — return 200 in milliseconds and process async via a queue — your handler's slowness must never timeout the provider's retry logic; and ORDERING — deliveries can arrive out of order — version or timestamp your events if order matters. WebSocket and webhook are complements: webhook ingests the world's events; WebSocket fans them out to live clients.

scenes.title: A verified, idempotent webhook endpoint
scenes.body:
import hmac, hashlib

@app.post("/webhooks/stripe")
async def stripe_webhook(request: Request):
    raw = await request.body()
    sig = request.headers.get("stripe-signature", "")

    # 1 · VERIFY — recompute HMAC over the RAW body.
    expected = hmac.new(WEBHOOK_SECRET.encode(), raw,
                        hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, sig):   # constant time!
        raise HTTPException(403, "bad signature")

    event = json.loads(raw)
    event_id = event["id"]

    # 2 · IDEMPOTENT — providers REDELIVER on timeout.
    if seen(event_id):                    # dedupe store (PY-21 Redis)
        return {"ok": True}               # cheap ACK, already handled

    # 3 · FAST ACK — queue the work, return 200 in ms.
    queue.push({"type": event["type"], "data": event["data"]})
    return {"ok": True}

# Handler (worker side): process queued events, mark event_id done.
# Out-of-order note: event['data']['created'] timestamps let
# you drop stale deliveries when order matters.
annot: HMAC over the RAW body — parse JSON after verifying, never before
compare_digest, not == — timing attacks are real on string compare
Return 200 fast, process async — the provider's retry timer is not your SLA

scenes.title: Hardening: heartbeats, backpressure, horizontal scale
scenes.sub: Demo sockets die quietly; production ones need a pulse
scenes.narration: Three production concerns separate toys from systems. LIVENESS: proxies silently kill idle connections — so the server pings (protocol-level PING frames or app-level heartbeat messages) every ~30 seconds and terminates sockets that miss two — without this, half your 'connected' clients are zombies. BACKPRESSURE: a slow client with a fast producer — broadcasting stock ticks to a phone on a train — buffers unboundedly in memory until the server dies; the fix is a bounded outbound queue per socket: full → drop, close, or degrade — never grow forever. And SCALE-OUT: an in-memory connection manager lives in ONE process — two replicas don't share sockets. Scaling options in order of complexity: STICKY sessions per replica (fine to ~10k connections); a PUB/SUB BACKBONE — replicas publish events to Redis (PY-21); subscribers forward to their local sockets — the standard at scale; or dedicated realtime infra (managed socket services) when that's not your differentiator. Design rule from AG-25: if sockets are your product's core, the pub/sub backbone is where you build; if chat is a feature, buy the last option and keep your team on the agent.

scenes.title: Heartbeat + bounded queue, the two survival patterns
scenes.body:
import asyncio

async def heartbeat(ws: WebSocket):
    """Kill zombies: proxies drop idle pipes silently."""
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(30)
            await ws.send_json({"type": "ping"})
    except (WebSocketDisconnect, RuntimeError):
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()

async def guarded_send(ws: WebSocket, queue: asyncio.Queue):
    """Backpressure: bounded queue, drop-oldest under pressure."""
    try:
        queue.put_nowait(message)              # never blocks
    except asyncio.QueueFull:
        queue.get_nowait()                     # drop the STALE one
        queue.put_nowait(message)              # freshness > completeness

# Horizontal scale — the Redis backbone:
#   replica A: event arrives → redis.publish("room:42", msg)
#   every replica: pubsub listener → forward to LOCAL sockets
# Connection state stays in-process; only EVENTS cross the wire.
# (PY-21 builds the Redis half of this picture.)
annot: Zombie connections are invisible until broadcast silently fails — heartbeats make liveness observable
put_nowait + drop-oldest: for live data, fresh beats complete — a 30-second-old tick is worse than none
Only events cross replicas; sockets never move — pub/sub decouples what processes own

recap: WebSocket upgrades HTTP into a full-duplex frame pipe — either side pushes anytime; delivery isn't guaranteed, so acks are your protocol's job
Connection manager (rooms/broadcast) + token streaming are the two patterns — async lets one thread interleave thousands of live connections
Webhooks invert HTTP: verify HMAC signatures on raw bodies, dedupe by event ID, ACK in milliseconds and process via queue
Production needs heartbeats (zombie detection), bounded queues (backpressure), and a pub/sub backbone (Redis) to scale past one replica

quiz.q: Why is constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) used when verifying webhook signatures?
opts: It runs faster than normal string comparison
Regular == leaks timing information — an attacker can measure response times to guess the correct signature byte by byte; constant-time comparison removes the signal
It's required by the JSON spec
quiz.why: == short-circuits at the first differing byte, so response time reveals how much of the signature was right. compare_digest always takes the same time — classic timing-attack defense (AG-23's security mindset applied to inbound traffic).

quiz.q: An LLM streaming endpoint takes 20 seconds to finish. Why must token streaming go over WebSocket (or SSE) rather than a single HTTP response?
opts: Chunked streaming exists, but WebSocket/SSE let tokens render progressively as they arrive — perceived latency drops from 20 seconds to first-token time, and the connection stays open for multi-turn interaction
quiz.why: GA-07's perceived-latency principle: users experience time-to-first-token, not total time. WebSocket (or SSE) streams partial results live; a plain response makes users wait for the whole answer. Plus the socket persists for follow-ups.

quiz.q: Your socket server runs two replicas behind a load balancer. A client connected to replica A needs an event produced on replica B. What's the standard fix?
opts: Make clients reconnect to whichever replica has the data
Store all sockets in a shared database
A pub/sub backbone (e.g., Redis): replica B publishes the event; every replica forwards published events to its own locally-connected sockets — sockets stay in-process, only events cross replicas
Disable the load balancer so all clients land on one replica
quiz.why: Sockets can't be shared across processes. The standard pattern: local connection manager + cross-replica event fanout via Redis pub/sub. (Sticky sessions work only until one replica holds too many connections.)

code.title: Realtime, end to end
code.body:
# The live pipeline:
#   browser ↔ WebSocket ↔ FastAPI ↔ LLM stream
#   world   → webhook  → FastAPI → queue → broadcast

@app.websocket("/live/{room}")
async def live(ws: WebSocket, room: str):
    await manager.join(room, ws)
    beat = asyncio.create_task(heartbeat(ws))
    try:
        async for token in llm.stream(await ws.receive_text()):
            await ws.send_text(token)          # tokens as they're born
        await ws.send_text("[DONE]")
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        pass
    finally:
        beat.cancel()

# Heartbeat in the background, tokens in the foreground,
# disconnects handled in the finally — a socket that
# survives production is a socket with all three.
annot: create_task(heartbeat) — liveness runs concurrently with the message loop
finally: beat.cancel() — no leaked tasks when clients vanish
This 15-line handler is the skeleton of every realtime GenAI app

notes:
# Real-time & WebSockets — PY notes

## WebSockets
- Upgrade handshake (101); full-duplex frames; delivery NOT guaranteed — acks live in your protocol.
- FastAPI: @app.websocket; accept/receive_text/send_text; WebSocketDisconnect is normal exit.
- Scale unit: connections, not requests.

## Patterns
- ConnectionManager: rooms → set of sockets; broadcast loops; prune on send failure.
- Token streaming: LLM async stream → socket; '[DONE]' sentinel; never block the loop.

## Webhooks
- Verify HMAC over raw body, compare_digest; reject bad signatures.
- Idempotent by event ID (providers redeliver); fast ACK then queue; watch out-of-order.
- Webhook ingests the world; WebSocket fans out to clients — complements.

## Production
- Heartbeat ~30s; two missed → close.
- Bounded outbound queues; drop-oldest for live data.
- Multi-replica: local sockets + Redis pub/sub fanout (PY-21).

## Cross-links
GA-07 (streaming latency), AG-19 (async jobs, idempotency — the same trio), AG-23 (secrets/trust), GA-28 (realtime voice rides these wires), PY-21 (Redis for the backbone and dedupe store).
